did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ecclesiastes presents wisdom as the ability to understand the “meaning of a matter”—that is, its significance or solution—and describes it as a power that brightens a person’s face and changes the sternness of his expression.
Did you know? In this verse, Ecclesiastes connects keeping the king’s command with an oath before God, emphasizing the duty of obedience and loyalty to authority.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes describes the king’s word as carrying great authority, so that no one can simply ask him, “What are you doing?”
Did you know? According to Ecclesiastes, there is an “appointed time and proper order” for every matter and action, but a person’s circumstances make it difficult to cope with reality.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes lists several limits to human control: no one can contain the spirit, control the day of death, escape from war, or be saved by wickedness.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes describes one person’s rule over another as something that can be “to his harm”—causing damage and suffering instead of benefit.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes explains that when the sentence for an evil act is not carried out quickly, people’s hearts become emboldened to do evil.
Did you know? Although a person may sin repeatedly while punishment is delayed, Ecclesiastes declares that in the end it will go well with those who fear God.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes calls it “vanity” that the righteous sometimes receive the fate deserved by the wicked, while the wicked sometimes receive the fate deserved by the righteous.
Did you know? In the face of toil and uncertainty, Ecclesiastes praises simple joy—eating, drinking, and rejoicing—as part of the life God gives a person amid his labor.
